This is a perfect Larry Sanders joke: it's character-specific (only a show-business obsessive would have 'C.A.A.' available as an answer where 'boyfriend' should be), structurally tight (long anxious pause + wrong answer), and it reveals character while being funny. Economy is near-perfect — two words and the joke is complete. Genuinely quotable within the show's fan community. Justifiably scores 8+.

jokes.explanation: The 'and hide that' is the hidden gem — we don't know what 'that' is, but the urgency implies something mortifying is visible. The specificity of the unexplained second command makes this funnier than a straight reaction would be.

dialogue.speaker: Larry Sanders
dialogue.line: The next time you bring Your father to the show, You tell him to keep His mouth shut, all right?

jokes.text: Of course not. / Good.
jokes.setup: Larry asks if the ratings were higher than his personal milestone
jokes.punchline: Artie gives a flat, possibly untrue reassurance and Larry's satisfied 'good' — the joke is that neither of them interrogates whether Artie is telling the truth, because Larry needs to believe it
jokes.explanation: The joke is in Artie's managerial flattery and Larry's willingness to accept it without verification. A tiny but effective button on Joke 41.

dialogue.speaker: Sharon Stone
dialogue.line: I don't think His depilatory problems Are my concern.

jokes.text: Norman: 'Larry, when you're dating Joanie Baloney, who gives a shit? But Sharon Stone — I'm wetting myself.' Larry: 'Well, that's a pre-existing condition, I believe.'
jokes.setup: Norman is explaining why Sharon Stone is special compared to Larry's usual girlfriends
jokes.punchline: Larry's 'pre-existing condition' response to Norman's incontinence claim is a precise, dry medical-bureaucratic deflection that also implies Norman is generally a mess
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. 'Pre-existing condition' applied to Norman's excitement-wetting is perfect deadpan — it treats a crude hyperbole as a clinical fact requiring HMO documentation. The economy is near-perfect (three words, complete joke), and it's completely Larry: dry, above-the-fray, dismissive. 'Joanie Baloney' is also a funny throwaway nickname. This is the Larry Sanders writing room at its best — sharp, quick, character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Larry Sanders
dialogue.line: ♪ Many a tear has to fall ♪ ♪ But it's all ♪

jokes.text: Norman: 'I need pictures of the two of you together. Hundreds of pictures of her. You're off to the side. She's blocking you. I mean, your ass is halfway out the limo door.'
jokes.setup: Norman is upset that the paparazzi photos from Morton's don't include Larry visibly
jokes.punchline: The specific image of Larry's ass halfway out the limo door while Sharon Stone's face is photographed is both visually comic and thematically perfect — he's literally being sidelined
jokes.explanation: A good visual joke told through description — the paparazzi photo where Larry is just an ass in a limo door establishes the episode's central theme physically. 'Your ass is halfway out the limo door' is a vivid, funny image.

dialogue.speaker: Larry Sanders
dialogue.line: I was on The wrestling team In high school, And I can break Any of your holds.

dialogue.speaker: Sharon Stone
dialogue.line: Yeah, well I know. I've seen your movies.

jokes.text: Norman mimes getting head-close to Larry: 'Next time they start snapping, get your head in close, you know? Just get it in like that, you know? That'd be better.' Larry: 'Why don't I just have her carry me around in a headlock?'
jokes.setup: Norman is coaching Larry on how to photobomb Sharon Stone's celebrity photos
jokes.punchline: Larry's 'carry me around in a headlock' reduction of Norman's advice reveals how undignified the whole project is
jokes.explanation: Larry's visible mortification at having to compete for camera space with a woman he's dating is both funny and sad — the headlock image is perfect. Good Larry deadpan with real bite about celebrity hierarchy.

dialogue.speaker: Larry Sanders
dialogue.line: You're at table 1? Mm-hmm. 1 what? Table 1. Who are you Sitting with?

dialogue.speaker: Sharon Stone
dialogue.line: Bill and hillary.

dialogue.speaker: Larry Sanders
dialogue.line: Oh, them.

jokes.text: Let me explain the second law of thermodynamics to you. Heat always passes from a hotter body to a cooler body and never the other way around.
jokes.setup: Norman is explaining why Sharon Stone's celebrity heat benefits Larry's show
jokes.punchline: Norman invokes the actual second law of thermodynamics as a show-business metaphor — which is both pretentious and surprisingly apt
jokes.explanation: Using actual physics — correctly — as a celebrity metaphor is a genuinely original and smart comedy choice. The second law of thermodynamics IS a good description of how celebrity heat flows. The joke is that Norman is both pedantic and correct. The follow-up 'Is there going to be a quiz on this?' confirms the room finds it as absurd as we do.

dialogue.speaker: Larry Sanders
dialogue.line: Table 1? [Sighs]

jokes.text: No. It's fabulous. I mean, you see, you're getting her heat, that means the show is getting heat, that means my kids will eat. / You have kids? / There are some kids in my neighborhood. Who gives a shit?
jokes.setup: Norman is explaining the heat-transfer theory in show business terms — 'my kids will eat'
jokes.punchline: When questioned about having kids, Norman admits he doesn't actually have children, just 'some kids in my neighborhood' — and immediately dismisses the distinction with 'who gives a shit?'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes, and one that reaches the 8+ threshold legitimately. The setup 'my kids will eat' is a standard rhetorical flourish about earning money. The reveal that Norman has no children — just 'some kids in my neighborhood' — is a brilliant subversion: the cliché turns out to be literally false, and then his dismissal of the distinction ('who gives a shit?') is both absurdist and darkly revealing. The logic is: he used a pathos-manipulation cliché, it was false, and he doesn't care. It's a perfect skewering of publicist rhetorical manipulation in three lines. Structure and originality are both exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Sharon Stone
dialogue.line: Are you actually telling me You couldn't get an erection Until you turned Your own goddamn show on?

jokes.text: Larry: 'If this is the way people react when I just have dinner, what's gonna happen if, god forbid, I have sex with her?' Artie: 'The shot heard round the world.'
jokes.setup: Larry is worried about the level of publicity attention his dinner with Sharon Stone has generated
jokes.punchline: Artie's 'shot heard round the world' frames potential sex with Sharon Stone as a historical/military event — perfectly calibrated bombast from a man of Artie's generation
jokes.explanation: Artie's Revolutionary War framing of Larry's potential sex life is very Rip Torn — grand, historical, deadpan. 'The shot heard round the world' is both perfectly quotable and a great character moment for Artie, who speaks in a register that makes mundane events sound epochal. Strong economy, very high character integration for Artie.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: If you're in A show business relationship, And the woman's More famous than you are, She's the one with the dick.

jokes.text: Do you know who ate the last doughnut? I'll kill the person who ate the last doughnut. Was it you?
jokes.setup: Phil has just asked 'did you bang her?' and seems to expect an answer
jokes.punchline: Larry's pivot to the doughnut — a classic deflection — is his way of refusing to answer, but delivered with genuine doughnut-rage that makes the non-sequitur land
jokes.explanation: The doughnut deflection is a classic Larry Sanders move — avoiding intimacy by redirecting to trivial workplace grievances. The 'I'll kill the person' is delivered with apparent sincerity, which is funny. It's also a structural mirror to the Cadillac fake-emergency deflection.

dialogue.speaker: Larry Sanders
dialogue.line: I can show you a list Of women this long That aren't famous That I haven't been able To get it up with. That came out wrong.

jokes.text: Unknown staffer monologue: 'I know that never in this lifetime will I enjoy the act of lovemaking with someone of Sharon Stone's caliber. I know this, and I accept this. I'm so fat.'
jokes.setup: A staff member is trying to get Larry to share details about Sharon Stone
jokes.punchline: The confessional escalates from philosophical acceptance of unreachable desire to a blunt, isolated 'I'm so fat.' — the non sequitur is devastating and funny
jokes.explanation: 'I'm so fat.' landing after 'I know this and I accept this' is a perfect dark-comedy beat. The speech builds to philosophical resignation and then collapses into raw self-pity in two words. The structure is genuinely good — the acceptance speech sets up the punchline's vulnerability with comic precision.

dialogue.speaker: Larry Sanders
dialogue.line: See, canyon ranch Is the female Equivalent To big bear. She's blowing Me off.

jokes.text: Staffer quoting scripture to get gossip from Larry: 'I am asking you to just take pity on me, please, just take pity and share with me some of God's bounty that he has obviously seen fit to bestow on you.' Larry: 'You sound like you're quoting scripture now. Are you aware of that?'
jokes.setup: A staffer is begging Larry to share Sharon Stone gossip
jokes.punchline: Larry's meta-observation that the gossip request has evolved into religious rhetoric cuts through the absurdity with a single grounded observation
jokes.explanation: The absurdist escalation of a gossip request into scripture is a good Larry Sanders bit — it comments on how Hollywood desire becomes quasi-religious. Larry's grounded 'are you aware of that?' is a perfect straight-man moment.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Larry, do you know I had this same Exact conversation With both your ex-wives?

jokes.text: Audience member heckles during the taping: 'How's Sharon?!'
jokes.setup: Larry has just finished what he calls his worst show ever.
jokes.punchline: The audience member's heckling 'How's Sharon?!' confirms the show's quality didn't matter — the only thing anyone cares about is the celebrity gossip.
jokes.explanation: A tidy ironic punctuation mark — Larry's professional humiliation (worst show ever) is compounded by public interest only in his personal life. Simple but effective industry satire.

dialogue.speaker: Sharon
dialogue.line: Sharon really Likes Larry, But she feels She needs to be involved With somebody outside Of show business. Somebody who can Nurture her.

jokes.text: Phil says 'That's the worst show we've ever done.' Larry says it was 'really well-received.' Phil: 'Are you insane? I thought you handled that heckler really well.' Larry: 'The next time you bring your father to the show, you tell him to keep his mouth shut.'
jokes.setup: Larry defensively claims the show went well; Phil contradicts him about the heckler.
jokes.punchline: The heckler was Phil's father — a reveal that lands as both a callback to the 'How's Sharon' heckle and a fresh absurdity.
jokes.explanation: The callback reveals the heckler was Phil's dad, which reframes the earlier moment delightfully. Larry's 'keep his mouth shut' is delivered with perfect aggrieved authority. A small but satisfying structural payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Boy, does he Crave attention.

dialogue.speaker: Beverly
dialogue.line: Yeah.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: He's taking it Badly, though.

jokes.text: Phil: 'That's the worst show we've ever done.' Larry: 'Are you insane? I thought you handled that heckler really well.' Phil: 'The next time you bring your father to the show, you tell him to keep his mouth shut, all right?'
jokes.setup: Larry praises himself for handling a heckler gracefully
jokes.punchline: Phil reveals the 'heckler' was Phil's own father — making Larry's graceful handling and Phil's apology both mortifying
jokes.explanation: A nice two-step: first Larry praises his own professionalism, then the reveal that the 'heckler' was Phil's father inverts everything. Phil's apology for his father asking about Larry's girlfriend is a good workplace-comedy beat. The misdirection (heckler → Phil's dad) is clean.

dialogue.speaker: Hank Kingsley
dialogue.line: I vote for a nurse. They can get You drugs, And those girls Really know How to swing.

jokes.text: Sharon is giving an interview backstage about Sylvester Stallone's love scene. Reporter asks: 'Did Sly have to shave for the movie? His chest? Wherever.' Sharon: 'I don't think his depilatory problems are my concern.'
jokes.setup: A reporter asks an increasingly inappropriate question about Stallone's body hair.
jokes.punchline: 'His depilatory problems are my concern' — Sharon dispatches the intrusive question with bored, upper-class precision.
jokes.explanation: The word 'depilatory' is doing enormous comic work — it's both the most clinical and the most dismissive possible response to a prurient question. The structure of 'Wherever' followed by that cold precision is perfectly timed. Sharon Stone playing a version of herself with this kind of weaponized elegance is a specific, well-executed joke.

dialogue.speaker: Larry Sanders
dialogue.line: She's not more famous Than I am, is she?

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: No!

jokes.text: Larry tries to look casual while waiting for Sharon's interview to end. Artie: 'You know, while I had to wait for Jackie Bisset, I used to stand there with a book and pretend I was reading.'
jokes.setup: Larry is hovering awkwardly near Sharon's interview, trying not to look like he's hovering.
jokes.punchline: Artie's advice — faking reading — reveals he has a personal protocol for dating-up-famous, involving Jackie Bisset. The absurdity of a practiced technique for celebrity waiting is very Artie.
jokes.explanation: The Jackie Bisset name-drop is not gratuitous — it positions Artie as a man who has navigated exactly this territory before. The 'pretend I was reading' is a wonderfully mundane celebrity-dating tip.

dialogue.speaker: Julianne Phillips
dialogue.line: Table 2.

jokes.text: Hey, I'm really glad to see the man's finally the one nude in the movie. I mean, if you're into that kind of thing. And I am. / Hear, hear!
jokes.setup: Artie comments on the movie Sharon Stone is discussing
jokes.punchline: Artie's 'if you're into that kind of thing. And I am.' — a double-take that first distances himself from the preference and then emphatically endorses it — combined with 'hear, hear!' from someone off
jokes.explanation: Artie's self-correction from fake-neutral to emphatic endorsement of male nudity is a quick, effective character joke. 'And I am' lands well. The 'hear, hear!' from off-screen is a good button. Not exceptional but solid.

jokes.text: Sharon's interviewer: 'Hey, I'm really glad to see the man's finally the one nude in the movie. I mean, if you're into that kind of thing.' Sharon: 'And I am.' Hank (or Artie): 'Hear, hear!'
jokes.setup: A reporter praises the reversal of typical Hollywood nudity dynamics.
jokes.punchline: Sharon's frank 'And I am' — unapologetic ownership of male objectification — followed by Artie's enthusiastic 'Hear, hear!'
jokes.explanation: Sharon's blunt 'And I am' works as a character moment — she's playing a liberated version of herself. Artie's 'Hear, hear!' is a small punctuation beat. Functional.

jokes.text: Sharon and Larry begin what appears to be a playful wrestling/flirtatious moment. Sharon warns: 'I have to tell you before we get started that I was on the wrestling team in high school and I can break any of your holds.' Larry: 'Yeah?' Then a flurry of exertion sounds: 'Unh! Unh! Unh!' Sharon: 'Wow! I only have one of those.' Larry: 'I could crush you.' Sharon: 'Yeah, I know. I've seen your movies.'
jokes.setup: Sharon warns she was a wrestler; they apparently grapple playfully.
jokes.punchline: Sharon's 'I've seen your movies' — in response to Larry's 'I could crush you' — reframes his physical threat as a comment on his cinematic presence/heft. The double meaning lands cleanly.
jokes.explanation: The physical comedy of the grappling sequence is a nice gear-change in the episode, and 'I've seen your movies' is a well-earned kicker — the ambiguity (is she impressed or is she suggesting he's a klutz?) serves the joke. Rewatch value comes from seeing the physical bit.

jokes.text: Larry invites Sharon to the Clinton dinner as his date, mentioning his two seats at 'table 20, which I understand is excellent.' Sharon says she also has tickets and was going to ask him as her date — but she's at table 1.
jokes.setup: Larry's proud offer of table 20 (established earlier as merely 'not bad') positions him as generous.
jokes.punchline: Sharon's table 1 — sitting with the Clintons — is the table-status callback that retroactively humiliates Larry's earlier 'not bad' seating and confirms the celebrity hierarchy dynamic.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's structurally strongest jokes — it pays off the table-20 setup from the episode's opening, uses celebrity status as the punchline, and lands as a story beat simultaneously. The escalating interrogation ('Table 1? 1 what? Table 1?') is perfectly written, and the final reveal 'Bill and Hillary' is the perfect name-drop punchline. The callback makes this significantly funnier on rewatch.

jokes.text: Larry invites Sharon to the Clinton dinner; she says she also has tickets. He asks where she's sitting. 'Table 1.' 'Table 1?' 'Mm-hmm.' 'Well, that sounds closer than my table.'
jokes.setup: Larry triumphantly offers Sharon his table 20 tickets to the Clinton dinner
jokes.punchline: Sharon's table is table 1 — with the Clintons — reducing Larry's 'terrific' table 20 to an irrelevance he can only acknowledge with 'well, that sounds closer than my table'
jokes.explanation: This is a beautiful callback payoff. The episode opened with Beverly and Hank assuring Larry that table 20 was 'not bad' — now it's revealed to be nowhere compared to Sharon's table 1 with the Clintons. 'Well, that sounds closer than my table' is the perfect Larry Sanders line: understated, pained, understated again. The slow revelation — 'table 1,' 'who are you sitting with,' 'Bill and Hillary' — is perfectly paced. High character integration: only Larry's ego would respond to 'I'm sitting with the President' with mild geometric observation.

jokes.text: Who are you sitting with? / Bill and Hillary. / Oh, them.
jokes.setup: Larry discovers Sharon is at table 1 and asks who she's sitting with
jokes.punchline: 'Oh, them.' — Larry's response to 'Bill and Hillary' as if they're mildly notable acquaintances he'd prefer to avoid — a masterpiece of performed nonchalance covering total ego collapse
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode. 'Oh, them.' is two words that do everything. It's Larry Sanders attempting to minimize the President and First Lady of the United States as a social obstacle he's mildly inconvenienced by. The gap between the words and their meaning is enormous — he's clearly devastated, but the construction of breezy dismissal ('oh, them') is peak Larry Sanders self-protection. Economy is perfect — not one wasted word. Character integration is essentially 10: no other character on television delivers this line this way. Quotability is the highest in the episode. This is the kind of joke that defines a character for the series.

jokes.text: Larry becomes visibly deflated after learning Sharon is at table 1 with the Clintons. He covers his ego collapse by fiddling with the radio: 'It's the radio. Let me... What's wrong? Nothing, what's wrong with you? Wait, I just gotta turn the radio off. There. All right. There we go.'
jokes.setup: Sharon notices something is wrong after the table-1 revelation.
jokes.punchline: Larry's transparent radio-fiddling — a physical manifestation of his ego crisis, desperately redirecting attention — is a perfect cringe beat. The repeated reassurances ('Nothing. What's wrong with you?') expose his fragility through denial.
jokes.explanation: Larry's ego-driven deflection — pretending to be distracted by a radio when he's actually falling apart over a seating chart — is quintessentially Larry. The physical business gives the actor something to do while the real comedy is his failing attempt to seem fine. High character integration.

jokes.text: Larry: 'Oh, well, I guess we could sit with them if you wanted to.' Sharon: 'Great.' 'What's wrong?' Larry: 'Oh, nothing. Nothing. It's not you, it's just... I don't-- It's the radio. Let me...'
jokes.setup: Sharon has just revealed she's sitting with the Clintons; Larry tries to play it cool and fails
jokes.punchline: Larry's total psychosomatic collapse — inventing a radio problem while clearly processing the ego hit — is a perfect cringe beat; 'it's the radio' for an invisible radio is inspired
jokes.explanation: Larry's 'it's the radio' is a quintessential Larry Sanders moment — the pathological need to attribute his psychological collapse to an external technical problem. 'Let me...' with no actual radio suggests he's pretending to adjust a radio that may not exist. The character integration is exceptional: this is Garry Shandling's specific flavor of male fragility made funny through complete commitment to the bit. 'There we go. There we go.' while doing nothing is a beautiful piece of comic mime.

jokes.text: Extended reaction beat: Larry stares at the ceiling alone, sighs, says 'Table 1?' to no one, then tries to recover: 'Well— Well, you're just tired, I guess.'
jokes.setup: Sharon has just revealed she's sitting with the Clintons at table 1.
jokes.punchline: Larry's silent, private devastation — talking himself down from an ego crisis with the inadequate 'you're just tired' — is the episode's most purely character-driven comedic beat.
jokes.explanation: This is the scene's emotional and comedic peak — the silent 'Table 1?' repeated to no one is pure character comedy. Larry's self-soothing ('you're just tired') is tragicomically insufficient for the scale of his ego wound. The moment functions as both comedy and character revelation, which is what separates Larry Sanders from lesser shows. The character integration score is very high because no other character in any other show has this particular wound in this particular way.

jokes.text: Table 1? / Mm-hmm. / [Sighs] / Well— / Well, you're just tired, I guess. / I don't know. / I'll tell you what... / Yeah. You're just tired. You're working too hard.
jokes.setup: After the table revelation, Larry and Sharon sit in an awkward silence as Larry processes the ego-blow
jokes.punchline: Sharon's gracious, slightly maternal reframe — 'you're just tired, you're working too hard' — treating Larry's status-wound as a fatigue problem, which is both kind and devastating
jokes.explanation: The pause-and-reframe sequence is strong cringe comedy. Sharon treating Larry's celebrity-status crisis as a simple tiredness problem is both condescending and sweet — she's being generous and he's being pitied. The awkward sighs before 'well—' carry real comedy weight in a no-laugh-track show like this. The scene is the best sustained cringe sequence in the episode.

jokes.text: Hank's voice on TV: 'And now, because he's better-looking than I am, Larry Sanders.' — playing on the TV in the background while Larry and Sharon are in bed.
jokes.setup: Sharon and Larry have put the TV on; it's The Larry Sanders Show.
jokes.punchline: Hank's on-air introduction of Larry — 'because he's better-looking than I am' — is the show's sardonic self-awareness leaking into the intimate scene. The meta-irony of Larry needing his own TV show to get aroused is the real joke.
jokes.explanation: The payoff — that Larry could not perform until he turned on his own show — turns the TV introduction into a dark, brilliant punchline. Hank's 'better-looking than I am' intro is funny standalone, but in context it's devastating: Larry's narcissism is so profound he needed himself on screen to function sexually. High character integration and originality.

jokes.text: Sharon, incredulous: 'Are you actually telling me you couldn't get an erection until you turned your own goddamn show on?'
jokes.setup: The revelation that Larry turned on The Larry Sanders Show to become aroused.
jokes.punchline: Sharon's direct, unvarnished articulation of what just happened — 'couldn't get an erection until you turned your own goddamn show on' — is the episode's most quotable punchline.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's comedic apex and one of the great Larry Sanders lines. The joke works on every level: it's an outrageous revelation, delivered in Sharon's frank, no-bullshit register; it perfectly crystallizes Larry's pathological narcissism; it's completely unexpected and yet feels inevitable in retrospect. The specificity ('your OWN goddamn show') makes it devastating — not just any TV, not even a tape of himself, but his live show currently on air. Could only happen to Larry Sanders, could only be said this way, and it's impeccably economical. Anchor-level moment.

jokes.text: Beverly walks in and protests the discussion: 'Gentlemen, please!' Phil: 'Look, he was being clinical. He didn't call it a woody.'
jokes.setup: The team is openly discussing Larry's erectile issue in a staff context.
jokes.punchline: Phil defends the conversation's dignity on the grounds that technical terminology ('erection' vs. 'woody') makes it clinical and therefore acceptable.
jokes.explanation: Phil's clinical-terminology defense is a nice callback to Beverly's earlier language policing, and 'he didn't call it a woody' is a perfectly absurd standard for workplace appropriateness.

jokes.text: Larry explains the sequence: 'Everything was going fine. We're in bed, terrific, and then I ask her if she wants to go to the Clinton dinner. And she says she's already going, and she's sitting with the Clintons. Next thing I know, all the blood in my body settled in my ass.'
jokes.setup: The staff asks what happened in the bedroom.
jokes.punchline: 'All the blood in my body settled in my ass' — the physiological description of status-anxiety-induced erectile dysfunction is both vulgar and weirdly precise.
jokes.explanation: This is an exceptional piece of comedy writing — the phrase 'all the blood in my body settled in my ass' is a genuinely original, vividly specific description of a psychosomatic reaction to ego deflation. It payoffs the table-1 joke with a physiological punchline. The specificity ('my ass' rather than anywhere else) is perfect. Highly quotable, could only be Larry's line, and the explanation retroactively makes the table-1 moment even funnier.

jokes.text: This has nothing to do with being famous. I can show you a list of women this long that aren't famous that I haven't been able to get it up with. / That came out wrong. / Take your time.
jokes.setup: Larry objects to Artie's theory that fame disparity caused his erectile dysfunction
jokes.punchline: Larry's defense inadvertently reveals a much larger pattern of erectile dysfunction with non-famous women — the joke is that his denial of one problem reveals a worse problem; 'that came out wrong' / 'take your time' are perfect buttons
jokes.explanation: One of the absolute best jokes in the episode. The structure is masterful: Larry defends himself against one charge and accidentally confesses to a far more comprehensive one — a classic comedic self-incrimination. 'I can show you a list of women this long' reveals the incident with Sharon wasn't anomalous, it's a pattern. 'That came out wrong' is the perfect internal acknowledgment; Artie's 'take your time' is a merciful and funny response that lets Larry sit in the hole he's dug. The escalation from specific incident to general condition is structurally impeccable. This ranks with the episode's very best jokes.

jokes.text: Artie: 'I warned you, didn't I? If you're in a show business relationship, and the woman's more famous than you are, she's the one with the dick.'
jokes.setup: Artie is being vindicated in his earlier warning about ego destruction when dating a more famous woman.
jokes.punchline: 'She's the one with the dick' — Artie's blunt, crass industry wisdom that reframes the power dynamic in aggressively crude anatomical terms.
jokes.explanation: Artie's maxim is genuinely quotable and incisive — it's simultaneously vulgar and astute. 'She's the one with the dick' as a power-dynamics metaphor is crude but precise, and coming from Artie it feels earned as hardboiled industry wisdom. High character integration (pure Artie, who expresses every insight in visceral terms).

jokes.text: Larry: 'It's only been a few days, and you know what? It feels like this relationship is all about her. This is not about me. I have no ident-- do you know what I'm talking about?' Artie: 'No identity.' Larry: 'Uh-huh. In this thing. It's all about her. Believe me, I know.' Larry: 'Not me. Sharon and who? Sharon and who?'
jokes.setup: Larry is describing feeling invisible in the relationship
jokes.punchline: 'Sharon and who?' — the rhetorical question reveals that Larry knows the answer and it's devastating: he's the unnamed variable in his own romantic life
jokes.explanation: 'Sharon and who?' is a beautifully self-aware Larry line — he's always the subject of his world, and now he's the unknown. Artie's 'no identity' as a clean completion of Larry's sentence is a good beat. The monologue is a bit long but 'Sharon and who?' is a keeper.

jokes.text: Larry: 'This has nothing to do with being famous. I can show you a list of women this long that aren't famous that I haven't been able to get it up with.' Beat. 'That came out wrong.'
jokes.setup: Larry is defensively denying that fame is the issue.
jokes.punchline: His defense inadvertently reveals a long history of the same problem, then 'That came out wrong' is his understatement of the situation.
jokes.explanation: This is a masterclass in escalation and self-incrimination — Larry tries to defend himself and instead reveals the problem is pervasive and widespread. 'That came out wrong' is the ideal closing understatement, simultaneously acknowledging the gaffe and not quite understanding how bad it is. Very Larry: his defenses always make things worse. Structure is near-perfect.

jokes.text: Larry: 'Not me. Sharon and who? Sharon and who?' Beverly on intercom: 'Larry, she's on line 2.'
jokes.setup: Larry is complaining that the relationship has no identity for him — it's always 'Sharon and...'
jokes.punchline: Beverly's intercom timing — announcing Sharon is calling precisely as Larry is mid-complaint about his anonymity in the relationship — is a perfectly timed situational irony.
jokes.explanation: The timing of Beverly's interruption — Sharon is on the phone exactly when Larry is bemoaning his invisible status — is a beautifully orchestrated situational joke. The structure (complaint → immediate ironic interruption) is clean and the delivery timing does the work.

jokes.text: The phone-call sequence: Larry is put on hold by an assistant, transferred to another assistant, then discovers Sharon is at Canyon Ranch — and each assistant apologizes and puts him on hold again.
jokes.setup: Larry calls Sharon's office, expecting to be put right through.
jokes.punchline: The increasingly humiliating chain of assistants, holds, and misdirections — each one more degrading than the last — becomes a comic metaphor for his diminished status in this relationship.
jokes.explanation: The escalating phone-hold sequence is sustained cringe comedy — each transfer and apology reduces Larry's status a little further. In a world where phone access = power, being bounced between assistants is a status indignity that lands as both funny and quietly painful.

jokes.text: Beverly explains: 'Canyon Ranch is the female equivalent to Big Bear. She's blowing you off.' — a direct callback to the episode's opening exchange about Larry using Big Bear as an excuse.
jokes.setup: Larry doesn't understand why Sharon going to Canyon Ranch is meaningful.
jokes.punchline: Beverly translates: it's the female version of the Big Bear blow-off excuse Larry himself uses — the callback perfectly closes the loop.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best structural moments — Beverly's 'Canyon Ranch = female Big Bear' pays off the cold open's Big Bear joke with perfect symmetry. Larry literally uses this tactic himself and now it's being used on him. The irony is both funny and thematically resonant. The callback earns its high structure score because it was planted early, developed through the episode's status dynamics, and paid off with Larry's own weapon turned against him. The earned vs. cheap score is very high because the payoff genuinely illuminates character.

jokes.text: Larry: 'I need to get out of this relationship. I need somebody who is not in show business. Someone who can nurture me.' Beverly: 'Larry, do you know I had this same exact conversation with both your ex-wives?'
jokes.setup: Larry declares he needs a non-showbiz woman who can nurture him — presenting it as a new insight.
jokes.punchline: Beverly's revelation that she's heard this exact speech from both his ex-wives exposes it as a pattern, a recurring episode of self-delusion, not a new realization.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's strongest character jokes — Beverly's 'with both your ex-wives' reveals that Larry's supposed revelation is a behavioral loop he can't escape, delivered by his secretary who has witnessed this cycle through multiple marriages. The high character integration score reflects that this joke only works because Beverly knows Larry completely and Larry doesn't know himself at all. Simultaneously dark and funny — it's affectionate, not cruel. Excellent structure (confessional setup → devastating institutional memory punchline).

jokes.text: Larry: '...well, that is a coincidence.' Beverly: 'Yeah, probably.'
jokes.setup: Beverly has just revealed she had this exact conversation with both his ex-wives.
jokes.punchline: Larry's 'that is a coincidence' — displaying complete inability to recognize his own pattern — is matched by Beverly's devastatingly dry 'Yeah, probably.'
jokes.explanation: This is the perfect tag to joke 49 and may be the single best-constructed two-line exchange in the episode. 'That is a coincidence' reveals Larry's total lack of self-awareness in three words, and Beverly's 'Yeah, probably' is one of the most economical, perfectly-calibrated sarcastic responses imaginable. The economy is near-perfect — two lines doing the work of a paragraph of therapy. Beverly's 'probably' does devastating work: it's not even worth arguing with him. Anchor-comparable for economy.

jokes.text: Beverly, in an extraordinary display of passive-aggressive diplomacy, calls Diane to break up with Sharon on Larry's behalf — telling Diane that Sharon feels she needs someone outside show business who can nurture her. Diane agrees.
jokes.setup: Larry wants out of the relationship and asks Beverly to handle it.
jokes.punchline: Beverly performs the breakup by attributing Larry's reasons to Sharon — essentially projecting Larry's exact complaints onto Sharon as if Sharon said them first. Both parties agree simultaneously.
jokes.explanation: This is a brilliant bit of situational comedy — Beverly solves the relationship problem by telling Sharon's assistant that Sharon wants exactly what Larry wants, using Larry's own words verbatim. The fact that both sides immediately accept the same reason reveals the mutual absurdity of Hollywood relationships. It's a minor masterpiece of sitcom problem-resolution that's also funny, ironic, and reveals how no one in this world communicates directly. High originality because the mechanism of the joke is genuinely clever.

jokes.text: After Beverly handles the breakup, Larry: 'Are you ok?' Beverly: 'Yeah, I just hate confrontation.' Larry: 'Sure glad I'm out of that.'
jokes.setup: Beverly has just executed a complex social maneuver while Larry sat passively.
jokes.punchline: Larry expresses relief that HE is out of 'confrontation' — when it was Beverly who handled everything while he did nothing.
jokes.explanation: Larry's 'Sure glad I'm out of that' — when he was never in it — is pure Larry: he delegates every unpleasant task and then experiences the relief as his own. Beverly's 'I just hate confrontation' is a small, sweet character detail. The irony of the deliverer of difficult news being the one who 'hates confrontation' is a nice inversion.

jokes.text: Beverly: 'I hope we've learned our lesson.' Larry: 'You ok?' Hank: 'I can't believe she's out of our lives.' Artie: 'All right.'
jokes.setup: The Sharon Stone relationship has just ended.
jokes.punchline: Hank's 'I can't believe she's out of our lives' — as if Sharon Stone dating Larry was Hank's relationship too — is the perfect Hank response: wholly self-involved while also being generous.
jokes.explanation: Hank's proprietary grief — 'out of our lives' — is a beautifully absurd response that reveals his parasocial relationship to Larry's dating life. His sorrow is genuine, which makes it funnier. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Artie: 'Boy, does he crave attention.' Then immediately pivots: 'You know, I need to meet somebody normal. Like a nurse or a schoolteacher.' Hank: 'I vote for a nurse. They can get you drugs, and those girls really know how to swing. When I was in for my hernia, I had a sponge bath, and whoa, baby!'
jokes.setup: The team is processing the Sharon Stone relationship fallout.
jokes.punchline: Artie's clinical diagnosis ('he craves attention') gives way to Hank's unsolicited hernia sponge-bath testimonial — a perfect demonstration of the 'craves attention' diagnosis being immediately illustrated by Hank himself.
jokes.explanation: The joke works on two levels: Artie's diagnosis of Larry is immediately self-applied to Hank (who launches into an anecdote about himself), and Hank's hernia sponge-bath memory as a romantic touchstone is wonderfully pathetic. 'Whoa, baby!' is perfectly Hank.

jokes.text: Artie introduces Julianne Phillips: 'I believe that's the lovely and talented Julianne Phillips.' Hank's panicked question: 'She's not more famous than I am, is she?' Artie: 'No!'
jokes.setup: The episode's entire arc has been about Larry's ego being crushed by Sharon Stone's superior fame.
jokes.punchline: The fame-status question now reappears in Hank's mouth — not Larry's — but Hank is asking about himself, revealing the ego pathology is systemic on the show.
jokes.explanation: A superb structural callback — the episode's central anxiety (is she more famous than me?) migrates from Larry to Hank, revealing that the narcissism isn't personal to Larry but endemic to the show's culture. Artie's flat 'No!' is also funny — he answers immediately and definitively, protecting Hank from Larry's fate. The callback elevates both jokes.

jokes.text: Julianne Phillips: 'Are you going to the Clinton dinner on Friday?' Larry: 'Yeah, I have a couple of extra tickets, actually.' Julianne: 'I've got 2 tickets. Where are you sitting?' Larry: 'Table 2.' — the episode's final line.
jokes.setup: Larry has just come out of the humiliation of table 20 vs. Sharon's table 1.
jokes.punchline: The table-number gag gets its final payoff — Larry has upgraded to table 2 (by Sharon's departure presumably freeing a slot, or simply by the natural churn), and the episode ends on the implication that this cycle is about to begin again with Julianne Phillips.
jokes.explanation: The episode's closing joke is an elegant structural achievement — the table-number motif (established at minute 0, deepened at minute 15, paid off here at minute 21) ends on Larry at table 2, still not table 1, still behind the celebrity curve, and apparently beginning the whole cycle again with a new famous woman. The economy is near-perfect: three words ('table 2') do enormous thematic work. The structure earns a very high score because this is the kind of payoff that reveals the episode was plotted with real care — the running gag was actually a thematic spine. On rewatch, every table reference gains weight.

tmdb_overview: Larry hits it off with guest Sharon Stone, but finds he can't cope with her greater celebrity status.
